tunelike-api.title: TuneLike API
tunelike-api.shortDescription: Social API for dating, live chat and city events — with a user portrait built from music taste.
tunelike-api.fullDescription:
TuneLike is built around a simple thesis: the music you listen to, the people you meet and the places you go are enough to draw a useful portrait of you. This API is the core of that product. It connects identity, live chat, dating, city events, media and recommendations in one backend.
The interesting part is how the modules feed each other. Playlist analysis and activity data shape a psychological profile. That profile influences who you see in dating and which events surface in your city. Chat exists in three forms — private, group and event rooms — so a match or a concert can become a conversation without leaving the platform. Events are not typed in by hand: Python workers scrape public ticket aggregators on a schedule and keep the catalogue current.
The service is an ASP.NET Core REST API on a Linux VPS, with Nginx in front, MongoDB for documents, SignalR for live messaging, and JWT plus Yandex OAuth for identity. Matching and swipe history sit in memory so the next candidate is cheap to fetch. Rate limiting, token revocation and structured logging are in place because this is a product API, not a tutorial.

auth.description: Identity is JWT-based, with email/password (BCrypt) and Yandex OAuth. Registration checks username and email; password recovery and token revocation are first-class; sensitive routes are rate-limited. Accounts can be linked to providers and flagged as verified. The controller stays thin — injected services plus a Swagger contract.

chat.description: Rooms are private, group (with admin and moderator roles) or tied to an event. SignalR delivers messages as they happen; a queue behind the hub keeps payloads if a connection drops. History is paginated, messages can carry attachments, and every action checks that the caller is actually a participant.

dating.description: This module owns profiles, preferences, likes, blocks and reports. Candidates are filtered and ranked; a match can also come from a shared event. Swiped profiles and active filters live in memory so the next card is cheap. Mutual likes become matches; either person can drop the match or hide the profile.

events.description: The catalogue is city-first: browse, filter, paginate. Python workers pull new events from public ticket aggregators on a schedule; the API then serves details, venue and who is going. One call toggles attendance. After the night, reviews and ratings feed quality back into discovery.

data.description: Activity and playlists are the raw material. The service records how people move through the app, pulls artist and track metadata, and groups music by attributes that later feed recommendations. Collaborative filtering turns that into event and content suggestions. Sharing preferences and anonymization sit next to the analytics, not as an afterthought.

utilities.description: Settings, notifications and privacy controls sit beside a referral loop — invite, reward, conversion — and a quieter piece: a psychological profile inferred from music taste. Email, logging and settings persistence cut across the rest of the platform so the product modules can stay focused.

simple-media-storage.title: Media storage API
simple-media-storage.shortDescription: Reusable image API: upload a file or a URL, convert to WebP, crop by saved recipes.
simple-media-storage.fullDescription:
Most small products need the same unglamorous service: accept an image, keep it safe, serve it fast, and crop it the same way every time. This API is that service. I built it once so the next product does not have to.
Files live on disk on a remote VM; metadata — owner, dimensions, size — sits in MongoDB. An upload arrives as a file or a URL. Images are capped at 1000 pixels, compressed, and converted to WebP at 75% quality. Responses carry ETags and cache headers so clients do not download the same bytes twice. Access is JWT plus policy-based authorization. Paths are generated on the server; uploads stop at 5 MB.
The distinctive piece is crop specifications. Instead of sending width and height on every request, you save a named recipe — size, algorithm, optional focal point — and the API produces consistent variants from it. Specs are ordinary CRUD resources. That is the difference between “resize this image” and a media layer a frontend can actually depend on.

imageProcessing.description: The pipeline is ImageMagick and ImageSharp on ASP.NET Core. Each item gets a unique id; the file lands in a structured folder; MongoDB keeps owner, dimensions and size. Incoming images are capped at 1000 pixels, converted to WebP at 75% quality, and may arrive as a file or a URL. ETags mean a client that already has the file does not fetch it again.

cropSpecification.description: A crop spec is a named recipe: width, height, algorithm, and a focal point when the subject is off-centre. You create, update, list and delete specs like any other resource. The API then cuts consistent variants without the client repeating the same numbers. That is what makes one crop reusable across screens and products.

css-cheatsheet.title: CSS Explorer
css-cheatsheet.shortDescription: Interactive CSS reference: properties and selectors, grouped, with a live editor.
css-cheatsheet.fullDescription:
CSS Explorer is a CSS reference you can use in the browser. Properties and selectors are collected in one place and sorted by topic: layout, flex, grid, animation. Each item shows how to write it and what it means.
Examples are live. You change the CSS on the page and the preview updates at once, so you can look a property up and try it in the same tab.
The layout works on a phone as well as on a desktop. It is built with TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind and shadcn/ui, and the site is public.

properties.description: Properties sit in collapsible groups — layout, box model, typography, flex, grid, animation and the rest — with syntax and a one-line meaning. You can open a group or scan the table. Browser support is a toggle, not noise in every row.

example.description: An example is not a screenshot of code. You edit the CSS in place and the preview updates at once. That is how the site earns a tab next to the docs: you try a value without leaving the reference.

selectors.description: Selectors live in a separate catalogue, beside properties. Same scan-friendly layout: what the selector matches, how to write it, a short note. Properties answer “what can I set”; this page answers “who does it apply to”.

mobile.description: The reference is built to work on a phone. Groups, tables and the editor collapse into a single column without losing the point of the page: look up a property, try a value, go back to the code.

dbclient.title: DBClient
dbclient.shortDescription: Windows app for a metallurgical plant: stock, clients, debts, and reports.
dbclient.fullDescription:
DBClient is a Windows desktop app I built for PROMEKZ, a metallurgical plant. The people who use it need one place for what is in the warehouse, what was sold, who the clients are, and who still owes money.
The app keeps stock by storage, records sales, stores the client list, and calculates bills, debts and deferred payments. Managers can look at a client’s numbers for a chosen period. Reports come out as Word, Excel or PDF through RDLC, and they stay editable. Every change is written to a session journal, so a manager can see who did what.
It is a WPF application on C# and .NET, talking to Microsoft SQL Server through ADO.NET and Entity Framework. There is a login screen, and the colour scheme can be changed. A short demo is on YouTube.

wpf-diagram-editor.title: Nodes
wpf-diagram-editor.shortDescription: WPF editor for flowcharts: shapes, text, connectors, export to XML, PNG and SVG.
wpf-diagram-editor.fullDescription:
Nodes is a Windows diagram editor. You put shapes on a canvas, add text, and connect them with lines and arrows. A picture you upload becomes a shape you can resize, so the palette is not limited to rectangles and ellipses.
The file you keep for later is XML: open it again and keep editing. When you need to send the diagram, you export PNG or SVG. SVG is a real vector path, not a screenshot.
I built it in my third year at HSE University, on the Software Systems Architecture course, in WPF with C# and XAML. The work that mattered was resize handles, connectors, and writing the canvas out as SVG.

3dstruct-editor.title: 3DStruct
3dstruct-editor.shortDescription: Draw lines in 2D, turn them into rounded 3D objects with splines and matrices.
3dstruct-editor.fullDescription:
3DStruct is a small modelling editor. You draw lines in 2D. The lines snap to each other. Then the editor turns that outline into a rounded 3D object: the shape is computed with splines.
Once the object is in 3D, you move it with matrix transforms. If you need exact numbers, you can edit the matrix yourself, not only drag on the screen.
It is a C++ application on OpenGL, for Windows. The interesting part is the path from a flat sketch to a volume, and the fact that the transforms are real matrices.

svo-airport-personnel-management.title: SVO — airport staff dispatch
svo-airport-personnel-management.shortDescription: Hackathon system: find the nearest qualified staff on the map and ping their phone.
svo-airport-personnel-management.fullDescription:
This is a hackathon project for Sheremetyevo airport (SVO). A manager has a problem — security, electrics, cleaning — and needs the nearest person who can actually do the job, not just whoever happens to be closest.
The Windows app shows staff on a map in real time. The manager picks a task and the skills it needs. The system finds people who match and sends a notification to their phones. Staff use an Android app that reports where they are.
Outdoors, position comes from GPS. Inside the terminal, iBeacons tell which floor someone is on. That is the hard part in an airport: GPS alone is not enough.
The dispatcher side is C# and Windows Forms. The phone app is Java on Android. Location is GPS plus iBeacon.
